article_content: At the 2013 Frankfurt Motor Show, Porsche and BMW unveiled hybrid supercars that challenge traditional expectations of fuel efficiency in high-performance vehicles. The Porsche 918 Spyder reaches 60 mph in under 2.8 seconds, delivers 887 horsepower, and achieves an impressive 72 miles per gallon—nearly a third more efficient than the Toyota Prius. Its all-electric range is 18 miles, and recharging is possible in less than seven hours using a standard socket, or just two hours with an industrial socket. The car's price is set at £537,000. The 918 Spyder boasts a carbon fibre body, a V8 combustion engine paired with an electric motor, and a total output of 887 horsepower. It can reach up to 211 mph, or 93 mph in all-electric mode. Porsche claims that its plug-in hybrid drive redefines everyday supercar performance and efficiency, combining near-silent operation with environmental appeal. The 918 Spyder set a new record at the Nurburgring racetrack, completing the 12.8-mile course in six minutes and 57 seconds—14 seconds faster than the previous street-legal car record. BMW's much-anticipated i8 hybrid supercar also made its debut, featuring a 1.5-litre turbocharged engine combined with an electric motor for a total of 362 brake horsepower. The i8 accelerates from 0 to 62 mph in 4.4 seconds and is limited to a top speed of 155 mph. It achieves up to 113 miles per gallon and emits only 59g/km of CO2. The i8 can run in electric mode for up to 22 miles at speeds up to 75 mph, and the battery can be charged to 80% in under two hours. With both a full charge and fuel tank, the i8 provides a range of approximately 310 miles. The car will be available for sale in July of the following year at a price of £99,845. BMW emphasizes the i8's innovative layering and aerodynamic design, made from a combination of carbon and aluminum, with characteristic blue accents. The company promotes the i8 as combining sports car performance with the efficiency and sustainability of compact vehicles. Both the Porsche 918 Spyder and BMW i8 demonstrate the potential for hybrid supercars to offer exhilarating performance while prioritizing fuel efficiency and reduced emissions, challenging the notion that eco-friendliness and driving excitement are mutually exclusive.

article_content: Roger Federer began his campaign for a fifth Australian Open title with a commanding straight-sets victory, even as he faced criticism from Rafael Nadal over his stance on players' rights. Federer, a 16-time Grand Slam winner, moved into the second round in Melbourne with a 7-5, 6-2, 6-2 win against Russia's Alexander Kudryavtsev, matching Nadal's smooth progression. World No. 172 Kudryavtsev, playing his first Australian Open, fought well early to reach 5-5 in the opening set. However, Federer overcame concerns about his back and dropped only four more games. Federer, 30, whose last major win was the 2010 Australian Open, will next face Germany's Andreas Beck, ranked 93rd. After the match, Federer emphasized his commitment to every point and reassured that his relationship with Nadal remains unaffected, explaining recent ATP leadership changes have caused some tension. Nadal, former world No. 1 and 2009 Australian Open champion, also progressed, beating American qualifier Alex Kuznetsov 6-4, 6-1, 6-1. Nadal had previously urged Federer to be more vocal on professional tennis player issues like scheduling. He later expressed some regret for making those remarks public, stating he maintains a good relationship with Federer. Nadal revealed that he needed an MRI after hurting his right knee during practice but was optimistic after his first-round win. He moved on to face Germany's Tommy Haas. Other players advancing included Juan Martin del Potro, Tomas Berdych, Mardy Fish, John Isner, Nicolas Almagro, Feliciano Lopez, Alexandr Dolgopolov, Stanislas Wawrinka, and Bernard Tomic. Top seeds Novak Djokovic will open his title defense against Paolo Lorenzi on Tuesday, and last year's runner-up Andy Murray will take on American Ryan Harrison.

article_content: REYKJAVIK, Iceland — Residents in southwest Iceland remain anxious as volcanic activity continues beneath the Reykjanes Peninsula. Authorities report that, even without an eruption, it could be months before evacuees from the affected zone can return safely. Grindavik, a fishing town with 3,400 residents, was evacuated last week after magma movements and thousands of tremors created a jagged crack through the area, pushing the ground up by over a meter in places. The Icelandic Meteorological Office indicates a significant likelihood of an eruption somewhere along a 15-kilometer magma tunnel, most likely near Hagafell, north of Grindavik. Grindavik lies about 50 kilometers southwest of Reykjavik and is close to Keflavik Airport, Iceland's main international gateway. The Blue Lagoon geothermal resort, a major tourist attraction, has shut down until at least the end of November because of volcanic danger. Evacuated residents are being allowed short returns—five minutes each—to collect valuables and pets. The volcanic system beneath the Reykjanes Peninsula, dormant for 800 years, has erupted three times since 2021. Previous eruptions occurred in uninhabited valleys and caused no damage. Iceland's location above a North Atlantic hotspot leads to an eruption on average every four to five years. The Eyjafjallajokull eruption of 2010 was especially disruptive, grounding flights across Europe due to ash clouds. Scientists predict any new eruption in the current area would produce lava, but not a significant ash cloud.

These incidents add to Mellor’s prior reputation for heated exchanges with service staff and public officials. Once known as the 'Minister for Fun,' Mellor’s legacy has been affected by both past scandals and these recent controversies.

A police manhunt is underway in Philadelphia after Christian Massey, a 21-year-old former football player, was fatally shot during an attempted robbery on Sunday. Massey was on his way to a friend’s house in the Winfield area when an armed individual confronted him, demanding his recently bought $300 Beats by Dr Dre headphones. Massey ran, but was shot five times in the back as he tried to escape through an alley, in full view of nearby children. 

The assailant ultimately left without taking the headphones, which were found next to Massey’s body. Grieving the loss, Massey’s grandmother, Eula Hodge, told NBC Philadelphia, "He was my child. Why did they shoot him when they didn’t even get what they wanted? He died over nothing." With no solid leads, detectives are calling for witnesses to come forward.

Friends and teammates posted tributes on social media, remembering Massey for his kindness and gentle spirit. Scott Todd called him “one of the most gentle, caring, and harmless young men I have ever known.” Steve Reynolds highlighted Massey’s importance to the Marple Newtown Tigers football team and his positive influence. Jess DiMambro recalled that Massey “always put a smile on everyone’s face” and sent condolences to his family.

A memorial service for Massey is scheduled for Tuesday evening on North Felton Street. The case has drawn attention to the popularity and high cost of Beats by Dr Dre headphones, which have become fashionable and lucrative items among young Americans since launching in 2006. Endorsements from top artists have propelled the brand’s success, making Dr Dre one of the world’s highest-earning musicians, with the company earning $110 million last year.

article_content: As the Uttarkashi tunnel rescue operation enters a critical stage, the families of the trapped labourers continue to hope for their loved ones' safe return. Haridwar Sharma, brother of stranded labourer Sushil Sharma, told ANI that they communicated with Sushil through walkie talkie on Friday morning, checking on his well-being. He confirmed that the workers have access to food, water, and clothing inside the tunnel and expressed his wish for a safe return. Sudhanshu Shah, brother of a trapped worker Sonu Shah, said that all their family members are anxiously waiting for Sonu, who has been trapped inside the tunnel for 12 days. He said Sonu remains courageous and is provided with essentials, including food, clothes, and toiletries. They spoke around 8:00 am, and Sonu is hopeful the rescue will happen soon. The rescue entered a critical phase on Thursday, with officials reporting that only a few metres remain to be drilled before rescuers reach the trapped workers. A technical issue with the platform supporting the Auger drilling machine briefly halted progress, but repairs were quickly made using an accelerating agent to strengthen the concrete platform, and work is expected to resume shortly. According to an official bulletin, a modified communication system with wire connectivity, developed by the State Disaster Response Force, allows for regular clear communication with those inside. The trapped workers have reported they are safe. Freshly cooked food and fruit are sent into the tunnel at regular intervals using a 150 mm diameter pipeline, referred to as the ‘2nd lifeline service’. The incident occurred on November 12, when a portion of the under-construction Silkyara-Barkot tunnel collapsed, trapping 41 labourers in a completed, reinforced area approximately 60 metres from the Silkyara side. Rescue efforts are ongoing as authorities focus on the workers’ safety and swift evacuation.

Il a confirmé que les ouvriers ont accès à la nourriture, à l’eau et aux vêtements à l’intérieur du tunnel et a exprimé son souhait de le revoir en sécurité. Sudhanshu Shah, frère de Sonu Shah, a indiqué que toute la famille attend impatiemment le retour de Sonu, coincé dans le tunnel depuis 12 jours. Selon lui, Sonu garde le moral et reçoit tout le nécessaire, dont la nourriture, les vêtements et des articles de toilette. Ils ont parlé vers 8h du matin et Sonu garde espoir que le sauvetage aura bientôt lieu. Le sauvetage est entré dans une phase critique jeudi, les responsables ayant annoncé qu’il ne restait que quelques mètres à forer avant d’atteindre les ouvriers piégés. Un problème technique au niveau de la plateforme soutenant la foreuse Auger a brièvement interrompu la progression, mais des réparations rapides ont été effectuées à l’aide d’un agent accélérateur permettant de renforcer la plateforme en béton. Les travaux devraient reprendre rapidement. Les ouvriers piégés ont indiqué qu’ils sont en sécurité. Des repas chauds et des fruits frais sont envoyés régulièrement dans le tunnel grâce à une canalisation de 150 mm de diamètre, appelée « deuxième cordon de sauvetage ». L’incident est survenu le 12 novembre, lorsqu’une portion du tunnel en construction reliant Silkyara à Barkot s’est effondrée, piégeant 41 ouvriers dans une zone achevée et renforcée, à environ 60 mètres du côté de Silkyara. Les opérations de sauvetage se poursuivent alors que les autorités accordent la priorité à la sécurité des ouvriers et à leur évacuation rapide.

Nadezhda Tolokonnikova, a 23-year-old activist and member of Pussy Riot, has reached her eighth day on hunger strike at a penal colony in Mordovia, Russia. She launched her protest in response to alleged death threats and severe work conditions, which her supporters describe as abusive. Her health has deteriorated to the point that authorities now prevent both her husband, Pyotr Verzilov, and her lawyers from visiting, citing her inability to communicate. 

Serving a two-year sentence for participating in a protest performance in a Moscow cathedral, Tolokonnikova insists she will not end her hunger strike until she is transferred to another facility. Her legal team has expressed fears about psychological abuse and filed a complaint with the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, comparing her treatment to modern forms of slavery. 

Tolokonnikova’s open letter exposing the conditions at her prison has fueled renewed debate about the treatment of inmates in Russia, especially women. Activists such as Lyudmila Alexeyeva have advised her to stop her hunger strike, believing she has already raised sufficient awareness. 

Prison authorities have cited minor offenses by Tolokonnikova, like failing to greet an official or refusing outdoor time, while her defense team continues to petition for her early release so she can care for her young daughter, Gera. Another member of Pussy Riot, Yekaterina Samutsevich, previously succeeded in having her sentence suspended, but Tolokonnikova remains resolute in her protest.

article_content: MountainBase, a ski company based in Morzine in the French Alps, is offering to pay fines of up to £700 for UK parents who take their children on a skiing holiday during school term time. The campaign, advertised with the slogan 'Are schools in the UK taking the PISTE?' highlights record snow levels in Morzine and excellent skiing conditions forecast. Currently, UK parents can face fines of up to £2,500, or even jail, for taking their children out of school during term time without authorization. The rules became stricter in September when Education Secretary Michael Gove eliminated the allowance for ten days of authorized term-time leave, except under ‘exceptional circumstances’. The new penalties begin at £60 per pupil per parent, doubling to £120 if not paid within seven days, and escalating substantially if not paid. MountainBase’s offer applies to any family booking in March or April (with certain exclusions), and the company promises to cover fines upon proof of payment. Defending the move in an interview on BBC Radio 5, company owner Lee Quince admitted the decision is 'irresponsible in one way,' but argued that the law, introduced to address truancy, is now impacting families who are not truants. He also noted that the company’s prices are almost 50% higher during school holidays, a result of supply and demand, and that accusations of 'ripping families off' are unfair. Quince explained that the company balances its year-round income and has budgeted for the potential cost of paying customer fines. A notable increase in fines—70% between 2012 and 2013—reflects the impact of the tightened regulations. Families argue that holidaying during half-term is often twice as expensive as just before or after school breaks. A petition signed by 170,000 people led to a parliamentary debate in February about the cost of family vacations during school holidays. Quince emphasized that parents are best positioned to judge if their children should miss school for a holiday and highlighted the unique value of sporting trips like skiing, which aren't available year-round in the UK. He suggested that broader issues in UK sports funding also contribute to this debate.

article_content: Thea Rhiannon recalls the man who came to her rescue decades ago. This account is part of the 'My Unsung Hero' series by the Hidden Brain team, which highlights stories of people whose acts of kindness made a lasting impression. One hot afternoon many years ago, Thea was driving her old Volkswagen bus down the highway. She rolled down her window for fresh air, and her car registration paper flew off the sun visor onto the floor. As she reached down to retrieve it, she inadvertently pulled the steering wheel to the left. When she sat up, she realized she had drifted into oncoming traffic. Panicking, she overcorrected, pulling the wheel sharply in the other direction. The van rolled over three times, and Thea was thrown onto the asphalt. "You were driving behind me that day," Rhiannon said about her unsung hero. "You saw the accident and stopped to help. When I regained consciousness, I was lying in the middle of the road, in shock and bleeding from extensive injuries." Rhiannon remembers the man as being in his late twenties, with a gentle manner, a calming voice, and kind hands. She does not recall his name, but he told her he was a medical student. "You stayed with me until the ambulance arrived," she said. "You covered me with a blanket and gave me emergency first aid, including placing a tourniquet on my left arm, above the area where it had been badly injured." At a hospital in Vallejo, California, doctors treated her injuries, removing glass shards from her arm and giving her dozens of stitches. The next day, she was told that, without the tourniquet, she would likely have bled to death before the paramedics arrived. "If by chance you see or hear this story and recognize yourself, thank you for your incredible kindness and compassion," she said. "I'm sorry it took me forty years to say this." Rhiannon also has a message for other unsung heroes who may not realize their impact: "Please consider this a pay-it-forward note of appreciation—from the strangers you helped, who, for whatever reason, couldn't thank you in person." 'My Unsung Hero' is also a podcast, with new episodes released every Tuesday. To share your own story with the Hidden Brain team, record a voice memo and send it to myunsunghero@hiddenbrain.org.
translated_content: Thea Rhiannon se souvient de l’homme qui lui a sauvé la vie il y a des décennies. Ce témoignage fait partie de la série « Mon héros méconnu » de l’équipe Hidden Brain, qui met en avant les histoires de personnes dont les actes de gentillesse ont laissé une impression durable. Par un après-midi chaud, il y a de nombreuses années, Thea conduisait son vieux combi Volkswagen sur l’autoroute. Elle a baissé la vitre pour prendre l’air, et son certificat d’immatriculation s’est envolé du pare-soleil jusqu’au plancher. En se penchant pour le récupérer, elle a accidentellement tiré le volant vers la gauche. Lorsqu’elle s’est redressée, elle s’est rendue compte qu’elle était passée sur la voie en sens inverse. Paniquée, elle a corrigé brusquement dans l’autre sens. Le van a fait trois tonneaux et Thea a été éjectée sur l’asphalte. « Vous étiez derrière moi ce jour-là », raconte Rhiannon à propos de son héros méconnu. « Vous avez vu l’accident et vous vous êtes arrêté(e) pour aider. Quand j’ai repris connaissance, j’étais allongée au milieu de la route, en état de choc et en train de saigner abondamment. » Rhiannon se souvient de l’homme comme étant dans la vingtaine avancée, avec une attitude douce, une voix apaisante et des mains bienveillantes. Elle ne se souvient pas de son nom, mais il lui a dit qu’il était étudiant en médecine. « Vous êtes resté(e) avec moi jusqu’à l’arrivée de l’ambulance », a-t-elle dit. « Vous m’avez recouverte d’une couverture et prodigué les premiers secours, notamment en mettant un garrot sur mon bras gauche, au-dessus de l’endroit où il était gravement blessé. » À l’hôpital de Vallejo, en Californie, les médecins l’ont soignée, retiré des éclats de verre de son bras et fait des dizaines de points de suture. Le lendemain, on lui a dit que, sans le garrot, elle aurait probablement succombé à une hémorragie avant l’arrivée des secours. « Si jamais vous voyez ou entendez cette histoire et que vous vous reconnaissez, merci pour votre incroyable gentillesse et compassion », dit-elle. « Je suis désolée d’avoir mis quarante ans à le dire. » Rhiannon adresse aussi un message à tous les autres héros méconnus, qui ne réalisent peut-être pas l’impact qu’ils ont eu : « Considérez ceci comme une note de reconnaissance à transmettre – de la part des inconnus que vous avez aidés et qui, pour une raison ou une autre, n’ont pas pu vous remercier en personne. » « Mon héros méconnu » est aussi un podcast, avec de nouveaux épisodes chaque mardi. Pour partager votre propre histoire avec l’équipe Hidden Brain, enregistrez un message vocal et envoyez-le à myunsunghero@hiddenbrain.org.

Indian equity markets opened flat with a modest positive bias on Wednesday, tracking mixed cues from Asian peers and divergent signals from domestic and foreign institutional investors. US Federal Reserve officials indicated that the central bank may be nearing the end of its policy tightening cycle, which supported a bullish outlook. The BSE Sensex traded 23 points, or 0.04%, lower at 64,918, while the Nifty50 was at 19,408, up 2 points or 0.01%, around 9:22 am.

Among Sensex stocks, ICICI Bank, Bajaj Finance, UltraTech Cement, Infosys, and Mahindra & Mahindra opened lower. In contrast, Asian Paints, Wipro, HCL Tech, Tata Motors, and Maruti began the day with gains. Apollo Tyres surged 5.5% following a more than two-and-a-half-fold jump in consolidated net profit to Rs 474.26 crore for the September quarter. Deepak Nitrite shares gained 5.2% after reporting a net profit of Rs 205 crore in the second quarter, with operational revenues reaching Rs 1,778 crore.

Sectorally, Nifty Pharma and Nifty Healthcare rose by 1% and 0.9%, respectively. Other indices such as Nifty Financial, Auto, FMCG, and IT also opened higher. In broader markets, the Nifty Midcap100 advanced by 0.75%, and Smallcap100 increased by 0.9%.

Globally, Wall Street equities climbed overnight as US Treasury yields declined after Fed officials suggested the end of the rate-hike cycle may be near. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite recorded their longest winning streak in two years. In Asia, technology stocks advanced but were offset by declines in commodity shares.

Market experts believe the current environment is favorable for a continued rally, despite ongoing geopolitical uncertainties. V K Vijayakumar, Chief Investment Strategist at Geojit Financial Services, noted the persistent tug-of-war between FIIs and DIIs, with FIIs continuing to sell while DIIs buy. He recommended high-quality large-cap stocks for long-term investors.

Aditya Gaggar, Director of Progressive Shares, highlighted a consolidation phase indicated by an inside bar candlestick pattern, with GIFT Nifty showing attempts to breach the near-term hurdle of 19,500 while maintaining support at 19,315.

FIIs remained net sellers on Tuesday, marking a tenth consecutive session of outflows with net sales of Rs 497 crore, whereas DIIs purchased shares worth Rs 700 crore.

Oil prices edged up slightly after hitting three-month lows the previous session, pressured by concerns over reduced demand from the US and China. Brent crude futures rose 4 cents to $81.65 a barrel, while US crude futures slipped 14 cents to $77.24 a barrel.

The Indian rupee appreciated by 2 paise to 83.25 against the US dollar in early trade, aided by lower oil prices and softer Treasury yields. The dollar index gained 0.06% to 105.6.

Meanwhile, India’s packaged consumer goods sector grew 9% by value and 8.6% by volume in the September quarter, driven by increased spending in rural areas for essentials and discretionary items, according to NielsenIQ.

Snap Inc., parent company of Snapchat, doubled its user base in India to 200 million within a year, supported by the popularity of its Spotlight feature, competing with platforms like Instagram Reels and YouTube Shorts.

India’s finance ministry has initiated talks on moderating the pace of capital expenditure increases in the interim budget for FY25 to align with fiscal deficit reduction goals.

article_content: Justina Pelletier, a 16-year-old from West Hartford, Connecticut who has Mitochondrial Disease, was recently admitted to a specialized medical center after her condition worsened. She was transferred last week from Yale-New Haven Children's Hospital to Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, a facility known for its expertise, where she is receiving intravenous nutrition and undergoing further testing. Previously, Justina spent 16 months in state custody at Boston Children's Hospital because of disagreements over her diagnosis. She was first admitted there in February 2013 with flu-like symptoms, but doctors suspected she was suffering from Somatoform Disorder, a psychological illness, rather than her family's stated diagnosis of Mitochondrial Disease. This misdiagnosis led to a prolonged custody dispute; Justina was placed in psychiatric care, largely isolated from her family and with limited outdoor access. Her parents, Lou and Linda Pelletier, consistently advocated for her physical diagnosis and care. They regained custody in June. After four months at home—including celebrations for her birthday—Justina’s health deteriorated, which led to her recent re-hospitalization. Mitochondrial Disease, which affects an estimated 1,000 to 4,000 children born in the U.S. each year, causes significant muscle and neurological problems and is very challenging to diagnose. Advocacy groups highlight that families in similar situations may face wrongful accusations of malingering or abuse. Psychiatric conditions like Somatoform Disorder also involve authentic pain without clear medical causes, making diagnosis complex and sometimes increasing tensions between families and healthcare providers. Justina remains hospitalized, and it is not yet decided when she will be discharged.

Elle a été transférée la semaine dernière du Yale-New Haven Children's Hospital au Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, reconnu pour son expertise, où elle reçoit une alimentation intraveineuse et subit des examens complémentaires. Auparavant, Justina avait passé 16 mois sous la garde de l'État au Boston Children's Hospital à cause de désaccords sur son diagnostic. Elle y avait été admise en février 2013 pour des symptômes ressemblant à la grippe, mais les médecins ont soupçonné un trouble somatoforme, une pathologie psychologique, plutôt que la maladie mitochondriale diagnostiquée par sa famille. Cette erreur de diagnostic a conduit à un long conflit de garde ; Justina s’est retrouvée en unité psychiatrique, souvent isolée de sa famille et très peu autorisée à sortir. Ses parents, Lou et Linda Pelletier, ont toujours maintenu qu’elle souffrait bien d’une maladie physique. Ils ont finalement pu la ramener à la maison en juin. Après quatre mois auprès des siens, dont la célébration de son anniversaire, l’état de Justina s’est aggravé, entraînant sa réhospitalisation. La maladie mitochondriale, qui touche entre 1 000 et 4 000 enfants chaque année aux États-Unis, engendre des troubles musculaires et neurologiques sévères et est très difficile à diagnostiquer. Les associations de soutien soulignent que des familles confrontées à de telles situations peuvent être injustement accusées de maltraitance ou de simulation. Les troubles psychiatriques comme le trouble somatoforme impliquent aussi une vraie douleur sans explication médicale, rendant le diagnostic complexe et parfois source de tensions entre familles et soignants. Justina est toujours hospitalisée et aucune date de sortie n’a été fixée.

article_content: Allison Williams impressed critics and viewers alike as she transformed into Peter Pan during NBC's live musical, Peter Pan Live!, on Thursday. The 26-year-old actress, best known for her role as Marnie on Girls, experienced a shaky take-off at the beginning, nearly colliding with a wall while demonstrating Peter Pan's flying abilities to Wendy. Williams quickly regained composure and continued her performance, which was praised across social media. The three-hour live production also starred Christopher Walken as the charismatic and quirky Captain Hook, whose performance drew both praise and some criticism, particularly regarding perceived lip-syncing. Nevertheless, viewers enjoyed Walken's tap-dancing and unique take on the character. The cast included Broadway performers such as Taylor Louderman as Wendy, Kelli O'Hara as Mrs. Darling, Jake Lucas as John, and Christian Borle as Mr. Darling and Smee. Alanna Saunders, a 22-year-old actress of Cherokee descent, portrayed Tiger Lily in a more culturally sensitive rendering of the character, with the once-offensive song 'Ugg-a-Wugg' updated to 'True Blood Brothers.' The production featured elaborate flying stunts, sword fights, digital effects like Tinkerbell and shadows, and a live dog. Notably, a brightly colored blue-and-purple crocodile captivated audiences and became a social media sensation. Celebrities including Lena Dunham, Katy Perry, Zach Braff, and Brian Williams voiced support for Williams before and during the performance. Social media buzz was high, with both appreciative and critical commentary — one common thread being praise for the vibrant production values and performances. Minnie Driver narrated the show and appeared at the end as adult Wendy Darling, delivering an emotional moment as Wendy allows her daughter to follow Peter Pan to Neverland. The show stirred nostalgia, emotion, and excitement among viewers. Peter Pan Live! followed the format of NBC's previous live musical, The Sound of Music, building on its success by incorporating more dancing and spectacle. While some critiques persisted regarding accent work and certain casting choices, the overall reception of Peter Pan Live! was highly positive, and viewers enjoyed the ambitious live broadcast.

article_content: In October, Indian tech startups secured just $538.4 million in funding—half the amount raised in the same month the previous year, based on Tracxn data. Most of these funds were directed toward seed-stage investments, totaling 92 funding rounds, a considerable decrease from last October’s 149 rounds and $1.14 billion raised. The ongoing ‘funding winter’ has been apparent since at least September 2022. Month-over-month, October’s numbers were also lower than September’s $870 million, marking a 38% decline. The number of deals fell by 21%. Seed and early-stage startups claimed 73% of October’s total, or $393 million. The top three investors during the month were Gruhas, Inflection Point Ventures, and Peak XV Partners. Highlighting notable rounds: InsuranceDekho raised $60 million in an ongoing Series B round with backing from Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group and BNP Paribas Cardif. Bizongo secured around $50 million in a Series E led by Schroder Adveq. Neo received $35 million led by Peak XV Partners, Fingerprint pulled in $33 million led by Nexus Venture Partners, and PMI Electro Mobility Solutions was backed with $30.1 million from Piramal Alternatives. On the regulatory front, Indian telecom companies claim that tech giants like Microsoft and Amazon are sidestepping legal telecom procedures by sending business messages via unregulated platforms like WhatsApp. This could be causing an estimated ₹3,000-crore annual revenue loss for both the government and service providers. The Ministry of Electronics and IT has invited Apple to participate in an investigation into alleged state-sponsored hacking attempts on iPhones belonging to several prominent Indians, including opposition parliamentarians. Lastly, the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) informed the Delhi High Court that Go First, a bankrupt airline, must allow lenders to reclaim leased planes and engines—complicating hopes for the airline’s recovery.

article_content: John Grisham, pictured in his Charlottesville, Virginia office, is releasing a new book: a sequel to The Firm, the novel that launched his literary stardom. Grisham has focused on steady output throughout a career spanning over three decades. "One smart decision I made was to hurry up and write," he said in an NPR interview. He has authored 49 books and sold more than 400 million copies, according to his publicist. Recently, he has joined a major lawsuit against the AI company OpenAI over copyright infringement (he declined to comment further). He has also voiced criticism of efforts to remove books from schools and libraries, calling such actions "ridiculous." Despite these controversies, Grisham prefers to spend his time writing. His latest book, The Exchange, is a sequel to 1991's The Firm, his breakthrough hit. When asked why he returned to The Firm after so long, he replied, "Well, we're always trying to angle a way to sell more books." The Firm was written while Grisham was practicing law and serving in Mississippi's state legislature. His debut, A Time To Kill, had a slow start, but The Firm became an overnight bestseller and was adapted into a 1993 film starring Tom Cruise – the highest-grossing R-rated film that year. Other books, including The Pelican Brief and The Client, were also turned into movies. Reflecting on his early success, Grisham credits his wife, Renee, and notes that they "kept our feet on the ground and we didn't change." He recognizes the cyclical nature of fame, noting, "Nothing is going to last forever. One day, this incredible journey will be over." As trends shifted in Hollywood, Grisham stayed focused on writing. The Exchange is set 15 years after The Firm, following Mitch and Abby McDeere as they live in New York City with their two children. The plot spans the globe, centering on a legal dispute involving a bridge in Libya connected to Col. Muammar Gaddafi. Early in the book, Mitch briefly returns to Memphis for a pro bono death row case, but the client dies before the case can begin—a thread that both recalls the first novel and highlights the recurring theme of injustice in Grisham’s work. In 2006, Grisham published The Innocent Man, a nonfiction account of a wrongfully convicted man. He now serves on the boards of The Innocence Project and Centurion Ministries, organizations that help free wrongfully imprisoned individuals. His forthcoming project is a nonfiction collection about people who have spent decades in prison for crimes they did not commit. Although his writing process and lifestyle have remained consistent, Grisham's trust in the legal system has shifted. "We're supposed to trust the police and prosecutors, and believe in judges," he said. "We want to believe the system always works, but it doesn't." Meghan Collins Sullivan edited the radio and digital versions of this story.

article_content: Supercars are notoriously attention-grabbing, especially when they are bright yellow, but a police officer couldn't avoid colliding with a Ferrari after an unsuccessful attempt at a u-turn. Witnesses were astonished as a silver BMW police car crashed into the back of a Ferrari 458 Spider, valued at about £250,000, on Edgware Road in London on Sunday night. A Metropolitan Police spokesperson noted it was too early to determine fault, but witnesses reported seeing the police car attempt a turn just as the Ferrari was reversing to pick up a friend. The police vehicle apparently did not notice the supercar reversing before the two cars collided, locking their bumpers. The Ferrari came off worse, with a large piece of bodywork left hanging off, while the police car suffered only a minor dent. The Ferrari's owner, who wished to remain anonymous, stated he was reversing at around 4 mph when the police car attempted a u-turn and struck his vehicle. He added that the police turned on their lights after the incident and subjected him to a breathalyzer test. 'It was quite a shunt, and I had to stand outside in the cold for two hours while they wore warm jackets. They didn't let me sit in a car,' he said, estimating the repair costs for his Ferrari could reach up to £30,000. A considerable crowd gathered to watch as the drivers exchanged details before the police vehicle reversed away with lights flashing. One bystander noted, 'I've filmed supercars across Europe for years, but this is the first time I've seen a crash like this involving the police.' The incident drew significant attention from the public, with many witnessing and filming the scene. A Metropolitan Police representative confirmed the collision, stating no one was injured and no arrests were made.

article_content: Kim Dotcom, the founder of the defunct file-sharing platform Megaupload, says he is broke and may be sent to jail in New Zealand. Appearing by video call from his luxury home, Dotcom claimed he cannot afford legal defense in his upcoming bail hearing. He said he has already spent $10 million on legal costs since he was arrested during a high-profile police raid on his mansion near Auckland in 2012. During the operation, authorities seized assets including cash, luxury vehicles, and firearms. Dotcom explained that his legal team has resigned, and that prosecutors are seeking to revoke his bail. Dotcom is resisting US attempts to extradite him over allegations that Megaupload enabled massive copyright infringement, allegedly earning $175 million from pirated movies, TV series, and other digital content. Authorities estimate owners lost over $500 million due to the platform. According to Dotcom, he can no longer draw on his resources to fight the charges, pointing out that his shares in his new tech venture, Mega, are now held in trust by his (now estranged) wife and their children. He expressed regret for forming a political party in New Zealand, which he said damaged his public image after intense criticism from government officials. Dotcom feels his conspicuous lifestyle—marked by expensive cars and private jets—made him an easy target for scrutiny. Dotcom admitted the combination of his public persona and Megaupload's services attracted both celebrity backing and controversy. While the site facilitated the transfer of large files, authorities maintain its main use involved illegal content. Subsidiary platforms were also shut down and more assets seized. He says that while he was once popular in New Zealand, official narratives have since made him a public outcast. Dotcom now fears that the upcoming bail hearing could result in his imprisonment.

article_content: The recent hack of Sony Pictures—allegedly by North Korean-linked hackers known as the 'Guardians of Peace'—has drawn widespread attention, with events unfolding like a Hollywood thriller. In the latest twist, U.S. theaters have canceled plans to screen 'The Interview' after the group threatened moviegoers with a 'bitter fate.' Beyond the headlines, the Sony breach offers valuable lessons in cybersecurity: 1) Not all cybercrimes are the same. The Sony hack, unlike common credit card theft or major corporate data breaches like those at Target or JPMorgan, was designed both to embarrass and to attract public attention, possibly linked to North Korea. It's vital to distinguish between different types of cyberthreats, as each requires specific responses. While some have labeled this incident 'cyberterrorism,' the FBI defines that as requiring acts of violence—a threshold not clearly met in this case. 2) No system is 100% secure. Even organizations with strong security practices can be breached. Companies must accept that intrusions will happen and plan accordingly, including protecting sensitive data internally, not just from external threats. 3) Email is never fully private. Sony executives seemed to believe their emails were secure, but any written communication can potentially become public. The advice to never write anything you'd be uncomfortable seeing published is more important than ever. 4) The cost of a cyber breach goes beyond technical fixes. Impact includes technical response costs, lost business, diminished customer trust, and damage to reputation, as Sony's experience shows. This is echoed in surveys of business leaders. 5) Attribution is complex and not always the main issue. While signs point to North Korean involvement in the Sony attack, definitive proof is hard to obtain, and knowing who is to blame doesn't always offer effective solutions. The focus should be on accountability, regardless of attribution.

Dernier rebondissement : des cinémas américains ont annulé la projection de « The Interview » après que le groupe a menacé les spectateurs d’un « sort amer ». Au-delà des gros titres, le piratage de Sony donne des leçons essentielles en cybersécurité : 1) Tous les cybercrimes ne se ressemblent pas. Le piratage de Sony, contrairement aux vols de données bancaires ou aux principales fuites de données chez Target ou JPMorgan, visait à embarrasser et à attirer l’attention, probablement sous l’impulsion de la Corée du Nord. Distinguer les différents types de menaces informatiques est crucial, car chacune exige une réponse spécifique. Certains ont parlé de « cyberterrorisme », mais selon la définition du FBI cela implique des actes de violence — ce qui n’est pas clairement le cas ici. 2) Aucun système n’est infaillible. Même les entreprises très sécurisées peuvent être piratées. Il faut anticiper l’intrusion et protéger les données sensibles à l’intérieur, pas seulement à l’extérieur. 3) Les e-mails ne sont jamais vraiment privés. Les dirigeants de Sony pensaient leurs messages sécurisés, mais tout écrit peut potentiellement devenir public. Le vieil adage de ne rien écrire que l’on ne voudrait pas voir publié reste plus valable que jamais. 4) Le coût d’une cyberattaque va bien au-delà des réponses techniques. Il s’agit aussi de perte de confiance, de réputation entachée et de perte de chiffres d’affaires, comme l’a vécu Sony, ce que confirment également des enquêtes auprès de dirigeants. 5) L’attribution est difficile et ce n’est pas toujours la priorité. Même si la Corée du Nord semble impliquée, la preuve formelle est rare, et savoir qui est derrière n’offre pas toujours une réelle solution. Mieux vaut se concentrer sur la responsabilité, quelle que soit l’attribution.

article_content: NEW DELHI: The Asian Development Bank (ADB) has approved a USD 100 million loan to enhance urban services and tourism facilities in Tripura. According to a release from the multilateral development finance institution, the project will upgrade urban water supply systems by installing 42 kilometres of new transmission and distribution pipes, establishing four new water treatment plants, and upgrading 55 kilometres of stormwater drainage. Additionally, the project will improve 21 kilometres of urban roads with features to meet the needs of the elderly, women, children, and people with disabilities. "This project will support Tripura as a gateway to the northeast region by developing tourist destinations along national highways and by improving urban governance and financial sustainability," said ADB Principal Urban Development Specialist Tomoo Ueda. To strengthen urban service delivery, the project will also build the capacity of twelve urban local bodies in planning, infrastructure operations and maintenance, financial management, gender equality and social inclusion, and project management. ADB will help upgrade tourist destinations including the Chaturdash Devata Temple, Kasaba Kalibari, and Neermahal Palace, through improved amenities, accommodation, landscaping, and by making these sites more visitor- and gender-friendly. The project will establish a digital museum and a new adventure park. According to the ADB, a 10-year tourism business plan will be developed to guide marketing and promotion efforts and to attract the private sector. The state's tourism policy will also be updated.

article_content: Murmurations—the captivating displays of thousands of starlings flying in unison—continue to intrigue scientists and nature lovers alike. Though the precise cause of this collective behavior isn't known, leading theories propose that murmurations either serve to protect birds from predators, such as hawks and falcons, or to attract more starlings to communal roosts, benefiting from added warmth and safety. Gretna in Scotland is renowned for its breathtaking starling murmurations. Recently, photographer Owen Humphrey documented a congregation estimated at 50,000 birds above the town. Meanwhile, the University of Gloucestershire and the Society of Biology are overseeing the UK's first nationwide survey of these spectacular events, encouraging the public to log details about any sightings—including location, bird count, setting, and duration. Dr Anne Goodenough, an expert in applied ecology at Gloucestershire University, notes that safety in numbers may explain the phenomenon and observes that only European starlings exhibit large-scale pre-roosting flights. As the starling population in the UK has dropped by 66% since the 1970s, data collected from this survey could help shed light on their behavior and the reasons behind their decline. Individuals wishing to participate can submit their observations at www.societyofbiology.org/starlingsurvey.

article_content: Debate is ongoing in Australia's political sphere about whether carbon trading is the best approach for tackling climate change. Carbon trading is considered a method for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Australian Prime Minister Kevin Rudd has proposed implementing a mandatory carbon trading system by 2010, which would cap the amount of pollution industries can emit. This system would be similar to the European Union’s emissions trading scheme, which began in 2005.  As the European system completes its first phase, Australia and other countries considering similar paths could learn valuable lessons. Carbon trading, also known as 'cap and trade,' sets a cap on carbon emissions and allows the trading of emission allowances. In such systems, a central authority—often a government—allocates emission permits, which can be bought and sold among companies or countries. Carbon credits can also be generated through investments in environmentally friendly projects, typically in developing countries.  The Fourth Assessment Report from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) provides strong evidence that human activities have caused global warming, altering climate through changes in seasons, rainfall, and the frequency of extreme weather. Industrialization has significantly increased greenhouse gas emissions, and the IPCC states that the average global temperature has risen by 0.74°C over the past century. If emissions continue at the current pace, the IPCC predicts an additional 3°C rise during this century.  Economic arguments regarding the costs of climate action—previously voiced by countries like the United States and Australia—have, at times, hindered progress, but carbon trading is promoted as a way to reduce emissions with minimal economic disruption.  The European Union Emissions Trading Scheme (EU ETS), established in 2005, is the world’s largest carbon trading system, covering about 12,000 facilities and representing roughly 50% of EU industrial emissions. Under the scheme, energy-intensive industries receive permits to emit specific amounts of carbon dioxide. Companies can purchase additional permits if they need to emit more or sell their surplus if they come under the limit.  In 2007, the EU ETS accounted for $50 billion of the $64 billion traded in the global carbon market, according to the World Bank. The UN’s Kyoto Protocol, in effect since 2005, also enables emissions trading and includes mechanisms such as the Clean Development Mechanism and Joint Implementation, allowing developed countries to earn credits by supporting emission reduction projects in developing nations.  New Zealand launched its own national system in 2008, and Australia plans to expand the New South Wales Greenhouse Gas Reduction Scheme nationwide by 2010. Japan and Canada are considering similar initiatives, while voluntary exchanges like the Chicago Climate Exchange also operate independently.  Carbon permit prices fluctuate based on supply and demand. In 2007, an EU permit for one ton of carbon traded at about $30–$35. Typically, the most energy-intensive sectors like power generation, steel, and cement manufacturing participate in these mandatory systems. Commercial aviation could be included in the EU ETS by 2011, while household and public transport emissions generally are excluded.  The success of emissions trading is debated. While capping emissions is considered progress, critics such as Carbon Trade Watch point to flaws, including over-allocation of permits. This was evident in the EU ETS Phase 1 when the market collapsed in 2006 due to an oversupply of allowances. Market analyst Franck Schuttellaar estimated that the UK’s highest-emitting companies gained about $1.7 billion from generous permit allocations.  Reports from organizations like Open Europe show that emissions actually rose in the UK and across Europe in the early years of the ETS. Proposals like auctioning carbon permits, instead of free allocation, aim to improve the system's effectiveness by increasing credit scarcity and incentivizing low-carbon alternatives.  Although carbon dioxide accounts for about 70% of greenhouse gases, a comprehensive mitigation approach should also include other legislative measures targeting a wider range of emissions.

Même si le dioxyde de carbone représente près de 70 % des gaz à effet de serre, une politique efficace devrait compléter l’échange de droits d’émission par d'autres mesures législatives couvrant toutes les émissions.

article_content: Kneeling on a pillow among mothers and their children, the Countess of Wessex looked at ease during a musical play session in Peterborough, Cambridgeshire, yesterday. She cuddled three-month-old Rowan Wilson-Jones and smiled as the baby sucked on her hand during a sing-along for toddlers. After greeting flag-waving pupils at Wittering Primary School, the Countess visited the children’s centre, which she renamed the Wittering Families’ Centre. The Countess, a mother of two, joined in nursery rhymes like 'Humpty Dumpty' and 'Incy Wincy Spider,' delighting families according to the community group who organized the event. She spent time rocking and playing with Rowan alongside his mother, Emma, appearing relaxed and friendly despite the baby’s occasional crying. Sophie crouched down to chat with enthusiastic pupils and parents in the playground. Earlier in the day, she visited RAF Wittering as Honorary Air Commodore. After arriving by helicopter, Sophie was greeted by pupils and given bouquets by two year-six students. She met with personnel in the officers’ mess, awarded medals and certificates, and spoke with families of RAF servicemen and women. Dressed in a black jacket, navy skirt, and nude heels, the 49-year-old royal represented both style and approachability. She stopped to tour a Grob Tutor aircraft and watched an aerobatic display alongside members of the Cambridge University Air Squadron. The Countess’s schedule has been busy, including charity suppers at Buckingham Palace, visiting the Royal School for Deaf Children in Margate, and promoting cancer awareness at the Pickering Cancer Drop-in Centre. In Tunbridge Wells, she toured the local hospital and unveiled a memorial to staff who died during the First World War. Next month, she is expected to visit Buckinghamshire, including the spinal injuries unit at Stoke Mandeville Hospital, while Prince Edward begins his own engagements starting in Birmingham.

article_content: Smoking and drinking often go hand in hand. Not surprisingly, when the cost of one increases, people tend to engage less in both. According to a study published in Alcoholism: Clinical & Experimental Research, raising cigarette taxes lowers both smoking and alcohol use—except for wine. The study finds that wine drinkers generally live healthier lifestyles and smoke less than those who drink beer or spirits. Researchers found that people who smoke are also more likely to drink beer and spirits, and when cigarette taxes rise, both smoking and beer/spirits drinking decrease. Higher cigarette prices correspond with lower rates of smoking and consumption of hard liquor and beer. "The results made sense to us because prior research shows that wine drinkers are less likely to smoke," explained Melissa Krauss, a data analyst at Washington University School of Medicine and co-author of the study. Using U.S. data from 1980 to 2009, Krauss and colleagues measured alcohol consumption per state and person, then compared it with each state's cigarette prices and public smoke-free policies. In 1980, the median cost of a cigarette pack was $1.76, rising to $5.68 by 2009. During those years, smoke-free policies became more popular, while alcohol consumption declined. According to NPR, states with the largest increases in cigarette taxes also saw the biggest drops in beer and spirits drinking: a 26% decrease in high-tax states compared to a 5% decrease in states with lower tax hikes. Researchers estimate that a 20% rise in cigarette prices leads to a 2% reduction in overall alcohol consumption. "We already know that stronger tobacco policies reduce smoking," Krauss said. "Now we see some positive, unintended public health benefits as well." Importantly, the study found that higher cigarette prices did not change wine consumption, likely because wine drinkers are less likely to smoke and often follow healthier lifestyles.

article_content: Gene Goldman is the Chief Investment Officer at Cetera Financial Group. Discover more insights from Cetera Investment Management (@CeteraIM). In the complex world of economic policymaking, data guides the Federal Reserve’s decisions. The Fed, which is the central bank of the United States, carries a dual mandate: to achieve maximum employment and maintain stable inflation. To fulfill these goals, the Fed reviews a variety of economic and financial statistics, helping shape crucial decisions that impact everyone. Understanding the Fed’s Dual Mandate At the core of the Fed’s mission is a careful balance. On one side, the central bank aims to ensure ample job opportunities, supporting a strong labor market. On the other, it is tasked with curbing excessive inflation, which can reduce consumers’ purchasing power. Interest rates are a primary tool for achieving this balance; the Fed can stimulate economic growth or slow an overheating economy by adjusting them. The Role of Economic Data How does the Fed decide when to change interest rates? That’s where economic data comes in. The central bank examines a wide range of indicators, focusing on three key reports for insight into economic health. The Non-Farm Payrolls report, released monthly by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, is a major indicator. It tracks employment, excluding workers in farming, private households, certain proprietors, nonprofit employees, and active military. This report offers a broad snapshot of job growth, with strong job numbers generally signaling a healthy economy. The Fed values this report because it provides one of the earliest looks at the previous month’s economic activity. While many people use the Consumer Price Index (CPI) to measure inflation, the Fed prefers the Personal Consumption Expenditures Core Price Index (Core PCE) for its inflation assessment. Core PCE is broader and more timely than CPI, so it offers a more comprehensive picture of inflation. Monitoring inflation is vital, as unchecked inflation can hurt consumer purchasing power and destabilize the economy. The University of Michigan's Consumer Sentiment Index is another key indicator, combining consumer confidence and expectations of inflation. Consumers drive close to two-thirds of the U.S. economy, so their outlook is significant. Pessimistic consumers tend to spend less, slowing economic growth, and changing inflation expectations can also alter spending habits. Predicting Economic Trends By analyzing these three main reports, the Fed gets a comprehensive view of the economic landscape. Current data suggests a possible economic soft landing: inflation appears to be slowing, and the labor market remains strong. Together, these factors point to economic stability and reduce the immediate risk of recession. However, the Fed does not limit itself to just these indicators. In reality, it reviews thousands of data points and emphasizes its 'data-dependent' approach. Investors should also look at a wide range of information, not just a few measures, when making decisions. The Federal Reserve’s use of economic data is central to its role in supporting the U.S. economy. By closely tracking many vital indicators, the Fed aims to achieve its dual mandate and maintain stability. For investors and economic observers, understanding these indicators can help in grasping the complex world of monetary policy. While no one can predict the future, it’s clear that economic reports will continue to be closely watched, and market volatility may increase. Dr. Anthony Youn, a plastic surgeon, recounts a memorable appointment with a Korean mother and her teenage daughter. The mother was insistent that her daughter needed to change her appearance by altering her nose, eyes, and eyelids. When Dr. Youn asked the daughter, Jane, for her opinion, she deferred to her mother, seemingly resigned.

Cosmetic surgery is especially popular in Asia, and South Korea stands out—with one in five women aged 19 to 49 reportedly having undergone a procedure, according to a 2009 Trend Monitor survey. While the United States and Brazil perform the highest absolute number of cosmetic surgeries, China and Japan follow close behind, and South Korea ranks seventh overall despite its smaller population.

There is less stigma in many Asian cultures associated with cosmetic procedures, and public figures, including Miss South Korea 2012, have openly discussed going under the knife. Interestingly, Dr. Youn observes that it is often the older generation who encourage such surgeries, sometimes pressuring their children to alter their appearances.

The most common facial surgeries—rhinoplasty and double eyelid surgery—are intended to create features more closely aligned with those typical of Caucasians. Asian rhinoplasty makes the nose narrower and more prominent, while double eyelid surgery adds a crease that is present in most Caucasians but only a minority of East Asians. While some professionals claim these procedures merely enhance attractiveness while maintaining ethnic features, Dr. Youn questions these motives, believing they cater to Western beauty standards, which he finds troubling.

Dr. Youn shares that earlier in his career, as a young surgeon, he performed these surgeries without much thought for the ethical implications. However, after encounters with families like Jane's and a request from an eight-year-old's mother, he began to critically assess the societal and personal reasons behind these procedures. Now a parent himself, Dr. Youn hopes his own daughter never feels compelled to alter the features she inherited.

He invites readers to reflect on these practices and share their thoughts, particularly on whether it's problematic for Asians to idealize Western features. The opinions expressed are those of Dr. Anthony Youn.

Le Dr Anthony Youn, chirurgien plasticien, raconte une consultation marquante avec une mère coréenne et sa fille adolescente. La mère insistait pour que sa fille modifie son apparence, notamment son nez, ses yeux et ses paupières. Lorsqu’il a demandé à la fille, Jane, son avis, elle s’en est remise à sa mère, semblant résignée.

La chirurgie esthétique est particulièrement populaire en Asie, et la Corée du Sud se démarque : une femme sur cinq, âgée de 19 à 49 ans, aurait subi une opération selon une enquête Trend Monitor de 2009. Les États-Unis et le Brésil pratiquent le plus grand nombre d’opérations, suivis de la Chine et du Japon. La Corée du Sud se classe au septième rang mondial, malgré une population plus faible.

Dans de nombreuses cultures asiatiques, le regard porté sur la chirurgie esthétique est moins stigmatisant, et des personnalités, comme Miss Corée du Sud 2012, en parlent ouvertement. Le Dr Youn note que la génération plus âgée encourage souvent ces opérations, allant parfois jusqu’à faire pression sur leurs enfants pour qu’ils modifient leur apparence.

Les opérations les plus répandues – rhinoplastie et chirurgie des paupières doubles – visent à donner des traits plus proches de ceux typiques des Caucasiens. La rhinoplastie asiatique rend le nez plus fin et plus proéminent, tandis que la chirurgie des paupières crée un pli, présent chez la plupart des Caucasiens mais rare chez les Est-Asiatiques. Certains professionnels affirment que ces interventions améliorent simplement l’attractivité tout en conservant les traits ethniques. Mais le Dr Youn remet en question ces motivations, estimant que cela aligne les standards de beauté sur ceux de l’Occident, ce qui l’inquiète.

Plus jeune, le Dr Youn reconnaît avoir pratiqué ce type de chirurgie sans vraiment réfléchir à l’éthique de ces choix. Cependant, après avoir rencontré des familles comme celle de Jane et avoir reçu une demande concernant un enfant de huit ans, il s’est interrogé sur les raisons personnelles et sociétales de ces interventions. Père aujourd’hui, il espère que sa propre fille ne ressentira jamais le besoin de modifier ses traits hérités.

Il invite les lecteurs à réfléchir à ces pratiques et à partager leur avis, notamment sur la question suivante : est-ce problématique pour les Asiatiques d’idéaliser des traits occidentaux ? Les propos exprimés reflètent l’avis du Dr Anthony Youn.

Every year, as winter approaches in Lahore—Pakistan's second-largest city—residents brace for the smog season, which brings a surge in allergies, respiratory problems, and even government-imposed lockdowns. Fourteen-year-old schoolgirl Eman Khosa dreads the onset of toxic air, sore throats, and being confined indoors. “Every year, when winter starts, smog arrives. The government takes some steps, and once the season ends, life goes back to normal,” Eman told Al Jazeera.

Her mother, visual artist Suraya Saleem Khosa, noted that while last year’s smog was less severe due to weather conditions, this year it is far more intense. “AQI [Air Quality Index] readings are sky-high. There’s no relief, no wind. Several poorly planned road projects are worsening the pollution,” she said.

Lahore, the capital of Punjab province bordering India and home to nearly 15 million people, is once again in the headlines for its hazardous air quality. This week alone, hundreds have reported illnesses ranging from allergies to serious respiratory issues. AirVisual, an international air quality monitoring agency, ranked Lahore as the world’s most polluted city for three consecutive days. AQI scores reached 406, 372, and 422 from Tuesday to Thursday, only dropping to 108 after a spell of rain on Friday before rising again to 152. For comparison, on Friday, London registered 25, Istanbul 61, and Mexico City 88.

According to AirVisual, the concentration of fine particulate matter in Lahore’s air peaked at almost 450—around 30 times the maximum daily exposure recommended by the World Health Organization. An AQI above 100 is considered unhealthy, and above 300, hazardous. Pakistan’s national classification is less strict, labeling AQI over 200 as unhealthy and above 400 as hazardous.

In response, the Punjab government declared a public holiday on Friday, creating a four-day break by extending the usual Thursday holiday. Public spaces, restaurants, and markets were closed, and officials called for a lockdown to improve air quality—keeping people indoors. Punjab’s interim health minister, Dr Javed Akram, said the extra holiday was intended as a one-off, aiming to reduce city traffic and, in turn, pollution. He largely blamed the burning of crop stubble by farmers in both Pakistan and India. “The biggest challenge is stubble burning, especially in India. We can’t control that,” he explained. Mohammad Farooq Alam, deputy director of Punjab’s Environmental Protection Agency, said stubble burning in India is at least five times more than in Pakistan, and shifting winds make it hard to manage. He added that the government is fining local farmers and exploring better disposal methods, though vehicular pollution also remains a major factor.

Alam also pointed out that weather conditions from October to late November trap pollutants closer to the ground, making the smog worse.

Climate change lawyer Sara Hayat agreed that the lockdown was necessary, but pointed out institutional shortcomings: “The government tries to act but can’t enforce its measures without building public awareness. These are temporary moves, ineffective without lasting policies.”

The shutdown has further disrupted the daily lives of Lahore’s people. Business owner Moazzam Maqsood reported losing "hundreds of thousands” of rupees (about $353 per 100,000 rupees) from closures. “We can’t open markets or staff the office. But staying home breathing polluted air hurts my health too,” he said.

Khosa, back at home with her daughter, said her air purifier helps reduce the smog’s physical impact but not the mental toll. “We stock up on masks and keep the windows closed, but mentally it’s draining. It’s dreary and depressing—we don’t look forward to autumn in Lahore anymore.”

Eman, after two years of pandemic lockdowns and online learning, misses going to school and resents the disruption to her education and hobbies. “We have exams coming up and need school for preparation, but now it’s closed. I love playing tennis in the evening, but can’t because that’s when the smog is worst. Some classmates have allergies or asthma. We barely get outside at all.”

Il n’y a aucun répit, pas de vent. Plusieurs projets routiers mal planifiés aggravent la pollution », dit-elle.

Lahore, capitale de la province du Pendjab, à la frontière de l’Inde et forte de près de 15 millions d’habitants, fait encore la une en raison de la toxicité de son air. Rien que cette semaine, des centaines de personnes ont signalé des maladies allant des allergies à des problèmes respiratoires graves. Face à la situation, le gouvernement du Pendjab a décrété un jour férié vendredi, prolongeant le congé habituel du jeudi afin de créer une pause de quatre jours. Espaces publics, restaurants et marchés ont été fermés, et les autorités ont décrété un « confinement » pour améliorer la qualité de l’air, incitant les gens à rester chez eux. Le ministre provincial de la Santé, Dr Javed Akram, a précisé que ce jour de congé était exceptionnel, destiné à réduire la circulation et donc la pollution. Il attribue l'essentiel du problème aux brûlages de chaumes après récolte, en Inde comme au Pakistan : « Le plus gros défi, c’est le brûlage de chaumes, surtout en Inde. Là-dessus, nous ne pouvons rien faire. »

Mohammad Farooq Alam, directeur adjoint de l’Agence de protection de l’environnement du Pendjab, estime que ce brûlage est cinq fois plus important en Inde qu’au Pakistan, et que le vent complique la gestion de la situation. Il précise que le gouvernement sanctionne les agriculteurs locaux et cherche d’autres solutions pour traiter les résidus agricoles, même si la pollution automobile reste un élément majeur.

Alam précise aussi que les conditions météorologiques d’octobre à fin novembre piégent les polluants près du sol, aggravant le smog.

L’avocate spécialisée dans le climat Sara Hayat pense que le confinement est justifié, mais constate des limites structurelles : « Le gouvernement tente d’agir, mais sans sensibilisation préalable, il ne peut pas appliquer ses mesures. Ce ne sont que des mesures temporaires, inefficaces sans politique durable. »

La fermeture perturbe encore davantage la vie des habitants de Lahore. L’homme d’affaires Moazzam Maqsood évalue ses pertes à « des centaines de milliers » de roupies (environ 353 $ par tranche de 100 000 roupies) à cause des fermetures. « On ne peut pas ouvrir le marché ni faire venir le personnel. Mais rester chez soi à respirer cet air pollué, ce n’est pas mieux pour ma santé », confie-t-il.

De retour à la maison avec sa fille, Khosa précise que son purificateur d’air allège les effets physiques du smog, pas son impact mental. « On achète des masques, on ferme les fenêtres, mais psychologiquement, c’est pesant. C’est morose et déprimant – on n’attend plus l’automne à Lahore avec impatience. »

Après deux ans d’école à distance à cause du Covid-19, Eman regrette la perturbation de ses études et loisirs. « On a des examens à préparer, et l’école est fermée. J’adore jouer au tennis le soir, mais je ne peux pas, c’est à ce moment que le smog est le pire. Certains camarades ont des allergies ou de l’asthme. On ne sort presque plus du tout. »

article_content: A new book by Tom Bower examines the challenges confronting business mogul Sir Richard Branson's space tourism venture, Virgin Galactic. The book asserts that Virgin Galactic may lack a sufficiently powerful rocket to carry customers into space and is still waiting for a full license from US aviation authorities, despite Branson's statements that flights could begin this autumn. Bower warns that Virgin Galactic is at risk of turning into an expensive 'white elephant.' He points out that the company has, so far, only managed a 20-second test firing of a basic rocket within Earth's atmosphere. During a recent test flight in California, SpaceShipTwo reached a maximum speed of Mach 1.4 and an altitude of 71,000 feet. However, Bower contends that further development is needed before tourists can be sent into orbit. According to Virgin Galactic’s website, the company has secured more than £42 million in deposits from around 580 individuals, and it has applied for a license from the US Federal Aviation Administration. Additionally, Chinese nationals have reportedly been banned from participating in Virgin Galactic’s spaceflights due to US anti-espionage regulations, given that the first commercial launches will take place in the US later this year. A spokesperson for Branson said Virgin Galactic has made significant progress, stressing that their scheduling prioritizes doing things correctly rather than quickly. Virgin Galactic, co-owned by Sir Richard’s Virgin Group and an Abu Dhabi investment firm, aims to become the world’s first commercial spaceline. Mojave-based Scaled Composites is developing new spacecraft (SpaceShipTwo, VSS Enterprise) and carrier aircraft (WhiteKnightTwo, VMS Eve) for the fleet. Journalist and investigative historian Tom Bower is recognized for his biographies of influential figures, including Robert Maxwell, Mohamed Al-Fayed, Gordon Brown, and Simon Cowell. He received the William Hill Sports Book of the Year Award in 2003 for Broken Dreams, an investigation into corruption in English football.

GUATEMALA CITY — Riot police in Guatemala began clearing roadblocks on Tuesday after President Alejandro Giammattei pledged to restore order to the country’s highways. For over a week, more than 120 roadblocks have disrupted traffic and commerce as thousands of farmers and members of Indigenous communities protest, demanding the resignation of Attorney General Consuelo Porras and expressing support for incoming President-elect Bernardo Arévalo.

Porras’ office has launched several investigations related to the August presidential elections and has successfully sought the suspension of Arévalo’s political party—actions that protesters view as attempts to undermine Arévalo before his January inauguration. At one major roadblock in the capital, dozens of riot police faced off with protesters. After a brief scuffle, police were quickly outnumbered by arriving demonstrators and the blockade remained.

On Monday evening, Giammattei announced in a taped message that he would seek the arrest of protest leaders, accusing them of receiving advice and funding from foreign sources. He labeled the protests as damaging to the economy and accused them of “vandalism,” expressing his firm support for Porras, who is sanctioned by the United States. Giammattei claimed that foreign funds had been used to support protest logistics such as food and portable toilets, and stated that both Guatemalan and foreign supporters would face arrest.

Protesters accuse the attorney general’s office of politically persecuting Arévalo, who has vowed to combat corruption and referred to the cases against him as an attempted coup. On Tuesday, Luis Almagro, Secretary General of the Organization of American States, described the actions of Porras’ office as “biased and irrational,” warning that they jeopardize the independence and secrecy of the vote and threaten Guatemala’s democratic stability.

Guatemala’s Foreign Minister, Mario Búcaro, argued that the protests have caused vandalism and harmed millions of Guatemalans, while Almagro maintained they have been largely peaceful, though vulnerable to criminal elements. Porras called for authorities to act against the mainly peaceful demonstrations, which have lasted for weeks as citizens demand her resignation over what they see as efforts to erode democracy.

The protests erupted two weeks ago after a turbulent presidential election. In a social media message, Arévalo accused Giammattei of endangering democracy by supporting the controversial attorney general and urged dialogue with the public. Arévalo and his Seed Movement party have faced increasing legal challenges and raids following their election victory in August.

Moves to suspend Arévalo’s party and steps against him have prompted Indigenous groups and rural residents to launch an indefinite strike, which started with 14 blockades and has now expanded to over 80 road closures nationwide. On Monday, Porras called the protests “illegal” and requested authorities forcibly reopen the roads. Both Porras and other prosecutors have been sanctioned by the United States, which accuses them of obstructing anti-corruption efforts and undermining Guatemala’s democracy.

GUATEMALA CITY — Mardi, la police anti-émeute du Guatemala a commencé à dégager les barrages routiers après que le président Alejandro Giammattei a promis de rétablir l'ordre sur les autoroutes du pays. Depuis plus d'une semaine, plus de 120 barrages perturbent la circulation et le commerce, alors que des milliers d’agriculteurs et de membres de communautés autochtones protestent pour exiger la démission de la procureure générale Consuelo Porras et exprimer leur soutien au président élu Bernardo Arévalo.

Le bureau de Porras a ouvert plusieurs enquêtes liées aux élections présidentielles d'août et a réussi à faire suspendre le parti politique d’Arévalo — des décisions que les manifestants considèrent comme des tentatives de le discréditer avant sa prise de fonction en janvier. À un barrage important dans la capitale, des dizaines de policiers anti-émeute ont affronté les manifestants. Après une brève échauffourée, les forces de l'ordre ont été rapidement dépassées par l'arrivée de nouveaux manifestants et le barrage est resté en place.

Lundi soir, Giammattei a annoncé dans un message vidéo qu'il chercherait à arrêter les meneurs des manifestations, les accusant de recevoir des conseils et des fonds de sources étrangères. Il a qualifié les manifestations de nuisibles à l’économie et les a accusées de « vandalisme », affirmant son soutien à Porras, qui est sanctionnée par les États-Unis. Giammattei a déclaré que des fonds étrangers avaient été utilisés pour soutenir la logistique des manifestations, comme la nourriture et les toilettes portatives, et a précisé que les soutiens guatémaltèques et étrangers seraient arrêtés.

Les manifestants accusent le bureau de la procureure générale de persécuter politiquement Arévalo, qui s’est engagé à lutter contre la corruption et a qualifié les poursuites contre lui de tentative de coup d’État. Mardi, Luis Almagro, secrétaire général de l’Organisation des États américains, a qualifié les actions du bureau de Porras d’« irrationnelles et biaisées », mettant en garde contre une menace pour la stabilité démocratique et l’indépendance du scrutin.

Le ministre des Affaires étrangères du Guatemala, Mario Búcaro, estime que les manifestations ont entraîné du vandalisme et nui à des millions de Guatémaltèques, tandis qu’Almagro considère qu’elles sont en grande partie pacifiques, bien qu’exposées à des éléments criminels. Porras a appelé les autorités à agir contre les manifestations généralement pacifiques, qui durent depuis plusieurs semaines alors que des citoyens réclament sa démission pour ce qu’ils perçoivent comme une atteinte à la démocratie.

La suspension du parti d’Arévalo et d’autres mesures contre lui ont conduit des groupes autochtones et des ruraux à déclencher une grève illimitée, débutée avec 14 barrages et qui compte désormais plus de 80 fermetures de routes dans tout le pays. Lundi, Porras a qualifié les manifestations « d’illégales » et exigé des autorités qu’elles rouvrent de force les routes. Porras et d’autres procureurs ont été sanctionnés par les États-Unis, qui les accusent de faire obstruction à la lutte contre la corruption et de fragiliser la démocratie guatémaltèque.

article_content: Robert Taylor, 36, was caught burglarizing a guest house just hours after being released from prison for a previous burglary. Taylor and William Shearon, 23, broke into the Kilburn Guest House in Bridlington, East Yorkshire, stealing a television, mobile phone, charity boxes for the RNLI, alcohol, cash, and the owner's Ford Mondeo. Taylor left his prison release form at the scene, which was later discovered by a neighbor among boxes of stolen items in the neighbor's back garden. The neighbor, alerted by barking dogs at 5 a.m., found the letter addressed to Taylor with details of his release, name, and address. Police were called and soon located Taylor and Shearon as they ran into the house of their friend, Daniel Kilbride. At Hull Crown Court, Taylor pleaded guilty to burglary, theft, and taking a vehicle without consent. He was sentenced to two years in jail and banned from driving for 12 months. Judge Michael Mettyear, the Honorary Recorder of Hull and the East Riding, commented on Taylor's record of more than 40 theft offences, noting that while drink and drugs may have played a role, it does not excuse the crimes or bring consolation to the victims. Shearon also pleaded guilty to burglary and handling stolen goods, receiving a two-year jail sentence. Kilbride was sentenced to nine months after admitting to handling stolen goods.

article_content: Forty countries, led by the United States, are set to sign an agreement to stop paying ransoms to hackers, in a coordinated effort to disrupt the financial foundations of cybercriminals. According to a Reuters report that quoted a senior White House official, the aim is to cut off the funds that ransomware operators rely on. Ransomware attacks have been steadily increasing around the world. The U.S. is particularly affected, making up about 46% of reported cases. Anne Neuberger, the U.S. deputy national security adviser focusing on cyber and emerging tech, emphasized in a virtual briefing that these attacks are likely to persist while criminals continue to receive payments. Ransomware operations typically involve hackers encrypting an organization's files and demanding payment for restoration. They also steal sensitive data and threaten to leak it unless paid. Major companies such as MGM Resorts International and Clorox are still dealing with the consequences of such attacks. The group’s key tactic will be sharing information about accounts involved in ransom payments. Lithuania will establish one of the two information-sharing platforms, while Israel and the UAE will collaborate on the second. The U.S. Treasury Department will help coordinate an international blacklist of digital wallets used by ransomware groups. Neuberger noted that artificial intelligence would be used to monitor blockchain activity and trace illicit funds. Chainalysis, a blockchain analytics firm, reported in July that crypto payments to ransomware groups could reach their second-highest annual amount this year.
